title: Modesty
description: Clothing, gender interactions, speech, and gradual growth without cultural pressure.

sections.heading: What to cover day to day
sections.content:
The rules on covering the body (awrah) apply all day, not only in prayer, and they apply to men as well as women.

For men, a Hanafi answer on SeekersGuidance says a man covers from the navel down to and including the knee, at all times unless there is a need. A SeekersGuidance answer on swimming says to go a little past the knee and suggests three-quarter compression pants. Check that sport shorts still cover your knees when you sit, bend or run. If they ride up, wear compression tights underneath. Men also do not wear gold or silk, and the questions page covers wedding bands and rings.

For women, a SeekersGuidance answer describes the covering in front of men who are not close relatives as everything except the face and hands. The Quran tells believing women to draw their head coverings over their chests (24:31) and to draw their outer garments over themselves (33:59). The schools differ on some smaller details, so ask your teacher which ones apply to you. The modesty and clothing guide has a section on starting hijab.

Covering also means clothing that is not see-through and not so tight that it shows the shape underneath. The SeekersGuidance answer on women's swimming, for example, asks for loose clothing that is not thin.

Both men and women are told to lower their gaze (24:30-31). A particular cultural garment is not the requirement. The covering is, and that is the target. If you cannot reach it everywhere yet, keep the step you can hold and plan the rest with a teacher.

sections.heading: Modesty is broader than clothing
sections.content: Modesty covers clothing, gaze, speech, behavior, humility, and dignity. Clothing is part of it and not the whole of it. Learn what modesty is for first, then take steps you can keep up.

sections.heading: Gradual clothing changes
sections.content: Start with what you can maintain: looser clothing, outfits you can pray in, or more coverage in settings where that is safe. Taking it step by step does not make what is required optional. Do not buy a whole wardrobe in a panic. Ask a qualified teacher what is required and how to plan the rest.

sections.heading: Grooming and the beard (fitrah)
sections.content:
The Prophet described a set of grooming habits as part of the natural way (fitrah). A hadith in Sahih Muslim (261a) lists ten, including trimming the moustache, letting the beard grow, cleaning the teeth with a tooth-stick, rinsing the nose, cutting the nails, washing the finger joints, removing underarm hair, shaving the pubic hair and washing the private parts with water. Apart from the beard and moustache, the list applies to women too.

Another hadith in Sahih Muslim (258) sets an outer limit: trimming the moustache, cutting the nails and removing underarm and pubic hair should not be left for more than forty nights. A weekly grooming day keeps you well inside it, and many people choose Friday.

The beard is where the schools differ. In Sahih al-Bukhari (5892) the Prophet said to let the beard grow and cut the moustache short, and Ibn Umar trimmed what went past his fist. A Hanafi answer on SeekersGuidance says keeping the beard is obligatory (wajib) in the Hanafi school, at about a fist's length, and that shaving it is prohibited. The same answer gives the Maliki view that shaving is unlawful. A Shafi'i answer on SeekersGuidance says the relied-upon Shafi'i position is that a full beard is recommended and shaving is disliked, not forbidden. It also notes that most scholars hold complete shaving unlawful, and that all agree shaving without an excuse is blameworthy. Ask your teacher which view you follow.

A beard is not a condition of being Muslim, and nobody should shame a brother whose job makes it hard. If your workplace requires you to be clean-shaven, talk to HR about accommodation before you decide anything. Ontario's creed policy (section 10.2) says dress and appearance rules must accommodate a religious beard unless that causes undue hardship. Its example is a bearded Sikh security guard. This is general information, not legal advice.

sections.heading: Culture and pressure
sections.content: Muslim cultures have different clothing styles. You may like the look of one of them, and liking it does not make it required for you. Be careful around people who shame you, compare you harshly, or treat visible changes as the only measure of faith.

sections.heading: Family, work, and safety
sections.content: Visible changes can affect how family reacts, and they can affect work or school. If a change might create hostility or danger, talk to a trusted local mentor before moving quickly. For workplace or school concerns, get qualified local guidance instead of relying on generic advice.

sections.heading: Close family you can relax your covering with (mahram)
sections.content:
Close family (mahram) means the relatives you may never marry. The list comes from the Quran. Quran 4:23 names the women a man may never marry, and Quran 24:31 names the men in front of whom a woman may relax her covering.

For a woman, these men are mahram:

- her father and grandfathers, her sons and grandsons
- her brothers, her uncles and her nephews
- her father-in-law, her son-in-law and her husband's sons
- her stepfather, once his marriage to her mother has been consummated (Quran 4:23)

For a man the list mirrors this: his mother, daughters, sisters, aunts, nieces, mother-in-law and daughters-in-law, and his stepdaughters once his marriage to their mother has been consummated. Foster (milk) relations can also make someone mahram (Quran 4:23). Ask a teacher if that applies to you.

Religion does not change any of this. A non-Muslim father, brother, son or uncle is still your mahram. SeekersGuidance answers in the Hanafi and the Shafi'i schools both say so, and the Shafi'i answer puts it plainly: mahram status does not depend on religion. Becoming Muslim is no reason to keep your father or brother at a distance, and hugging a parent or sibling is not the problem.

Cousins are not mahram. Neither are brothers-in-law and sisters-in-law, step-siblings, or a friend's parents, because none of them are on these lists. The Prophet (peace be upon him) warned about a husband's relatives in particular (Sahih al-Bukhari 5232), so take extra care there. He also said a man should not be alone with a woman unless a mahram is with her (Sahih al-Bukhari 5233).

At family gatherings, you can relax your covering at home with mahram relatives. The Hanafi answer adds: unless you have reason to worry about how someone behaves. With cousins and in-laws, keep things friendly and in company. Help in the kitchen with everyone, sit with the group, and enjoy the day, without going off alone with one of them.

Safety comes first. Being mahram never obliges you to be alone with, or travel with, someone who is unsafe. A Hanafi answer from SeekersGuidance says this about stepfathers and siblings too.

**Where scholars differ:** the Hanafi answer allows a woman to travel with, or be alone with, a non-Muslim mahram who is not morally corrupt. The other schools were not checked for this guide. For a stepfather, one Hanafi answer says he is mahram when he is married to your mother and raised you, while Quran 4:23 ties the step-relationship to the marriage with your mother being consummated. Sketch your family tree and go through it with a qualified teacher, privately if you prefer.
